A 2,000-year-old tomb was discovered in an elite burial ground of the Xiongnu, some of whom were the ancestors of the Huns.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia.

Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia.

Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East.

When the Xiongnu Empire fractured in the late first century B.C., one band moved west, picking up new tribes and eventually becoming the horde known as the Huns. Both the Xiongnu and the Huns were well known for their fighting and horseback riding skills.

The newly announced tomb is roughly square, with a long passageway extending from it, according to the statement. Including the passageway, the tomb is about 240 feet (73 meters) long, roughly the size of the Great Sphinx of Giza. Archaeologists discovered nine concentric layers of stone, each smaller than the last, going down around 48 feet (14.5 m) deep, making the tomb a kind of inverted pyramid.

Jade "bi" discs unearthed on the floor of the coffin.

A glass cup with a handle, possibly made in the Roman Empire.

Archaeologists unearthed a wooden carriage from one of the tomb layers.

In the tomb's central chamber, archaeologists found a wooden burial chamber with a coffin. The burial chamber is smaller than other elite Xiongnu burials, according to the statement, which may suggest that the society was changing and Xiongnu power was declining when the tomb was created in the late first to second century A.D.

Artifacts found in the tomb show the extent of the Xiongnu's connections across Eurasia 2,000 years ago, according to the statement. Among the grave goods recovered from the tomb were silver-and-quartz accessories crafted to decorate horses, as well as a wheel from a lacquered horse-drawn carriage, suggesting the tomb's occupant was a person of high social status.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Additionally, archaeologists found evidence of connections with the Han dynasty, which arose around 200 B.C. and was the second imperial dynasty of ancient China. On the bottom of the wooden coffin, archaeologists recovered 15 flat, overlapping pieces of jade.

Han dynasty burials of important people often included at least one "bi," the term for a jade disk. But unlike the typically circular "bi," the jade pieces in the Xiongnu tomb are irregular and have elaborate designs engraved on them, according to the statement. This may suggest that the Xiongnu adopted a Han burial practice but put their own spin on it.

Archaeologists also found a broken cup in the tomb. The transparent glass cup with a handle may have been manufactured in the Roman Empire, the archaeologists believe. Additional tests will be carried out to try to determine where the glass cup was made.

So far, archaeologists are unsure who was buried in the tomb. But they plan to use DNA analysis techniques on the teeth and hair they recovered from the coffin to figure out the person's chromosomal sex and whether the individual was related to other people interred in the Duurlig Nars burial complex. According to the statement, future analyses of this important tomb will help archaeologists paint a more detailed picture of ancient Xiongnu society two millennia ago.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6357. Locusts may help scientists detect hard-to-treat lung infections

In lab tests, locusts could smell the difference between bacterial biofilms and free-floating bacteria, a finding that could inform future breath tests.

Bacteria become much harder to kill once they attach to a surface and build a slimy protective layer.

These colonies are called biofilms. No test can currently detect them in a patient’s lungs without an invasive procedure.

A locust’s sense of smell might help one day.

In lab tests, researchers used signals from locust brains to tell biofilms apart from free-floating bacteria of the same species by smell.

The clearest signal appeared about a second after the odor reached the locusts’ antennae.

Debajit Saha and Jonathan Hardy were the senior authors of the study. Both are associate professors at Michigan State University (MSU). Michael Parnas was the first author.

Saha works in the College of Engineering. Hardy is based in the Department of Microbiology, Genetics and Immunology. Both researchers also belong to MSU’s Institute for Quantitative Health Science and Engineering.

Only bacterial cultures grown in flasks were used. Breath samples and patients were not tested.

Saha noted that before the experiments, it was not clear that an odor alone could show how bacteria were growing.

“Seeing such a high level of discrimination was therefore quite surprising,” Saha said.

A biofilm forms when bacteria settle on a solid surface. A sticky coating is then built around the whole colony.

Inside that coating, bacteria can be up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics than free-floating bacteria. The authors gave that figure in the paper.

Some bacteria deep in the colony have a slower metabolism. Those cells can survive treatment, and the biofilm is rebuilt afterward.

Biofilms account for about 80% of bacterial infections in people, according to earlier research cited in the paper. Wounds, implants and the lungs can all be affected.

An infection is usually identified by growing a sample in a laboratory. That process takes a few days. Faster tests exist, but they cannot separate a biofilm from free-floating bacteria.

Bacteria also release chemicals into the air as they grow. Together, those airborne chemicals form an odor. An odor can be sampled from outside the body.

Locusts smell with their antennae. More than 100,000 odor-sensing nerve cells are found on each antenna.

The signals from those cells all pass through about 800 output neurons. These neurons are located in one small smell-processing region of the brain.

For the experiment, the brain was surgically exposed in six living locusts. Each insect was held still, and an electrode was placed in that region.

The team then blew air from five flasks across the antennae. Four flasks contained bacteria. The fifth contained only the broth in which the bacteria had been grown.

Two species were used, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Each species was grown in two ways, as a biofilm and as a free-floating culture.

Each odor was delivered for four seconds and repeated five times, with one minute between deliveries. The activity of 32 neurons was isolated from the recordings.

The locusts had not been trained on these odors. Insect brains have been used this way by Saha’s lab before. In earlier work, recordings were taken from locusts and honeybees exposed to the odors of human cancer cells.

Trained dogs can also detect some diseases by smell. However, a test based on an animal’s behavior gives only a yes or a no, the authors wrote.

A computer program compared the firing pattern from each trial with the patterns from the other trials. The closest match was then selected.

When all five odors were included, 22 of 25 trials were matched to the correct flask. That is an accuracy of 88%. Guessing would be right only 20% of the time.

Both biofilms were identified in every trial.

One of the five free-floating Staphylococcus trials was mistaken for the Staphylococcus biofilm. The plain broth was also mistaken for a Staphylococcus odor twice.

In this analysis, every biofilm was caught by the program. One free-floating sample was wrongly flagged as a biofilm, however.

The researchers reported accuracy of up to 96% when individual biofilm and free-floating odors were classified.

The largest differences in firing patterns were seen between the two species. Biofilm and free-floating cultures of the same species produced more similar patterns. Even so, they were still separated by the recordings.

Saha said bacteria release a different mix of airborne chemicals when their growth state changes. These subtle changes can be picked up by the insects.

Before the odor arrived, the program performed no better than guessing. Accuracy rose quickly once the odor was delivered.

The team then tested how little brain activity was needed. A half-second slice of the recording was enough for 91% accuracy. That slice was centered about one second after the odor arrived.

A quarter-second slice from the same moment gave 82% accuracy. A laboratory culture, by comparison, takes days.

The 32 neurons represent about 4% of the roughly 800 output neurons in the smell-processing region. The biofilm analysis was also repeated on random subsets of the 32.

Performance improved as more neurons were included.

Only one laboratory strain of each species was used. Human breath is more complicated. It also carries chemicals from food, medications and the surrounding air.

Several other limits were listed by the authors. The number of bacteria could not be kept exactly equal in the biofilm and free-floating flasks. That difference alone could change an odor.

All 32 neurons were pooled from six insects. The study therefore does not show a single locust doing the job.

The recordings stayed strong for about four hours after surgery. How long a locust lasts as a sensor depends on its health and the surgeon’s skill, the authors wrote.

Drug-resistant strains such as MRSA were not tested either. The team expects those strains to be harder to distinguish from ordinary Staphylococcus.

No one has yet tested whether a locust brain can pick a biofilm’s odor out of human breath.

Breath studies are the next step, the authors wrote. Hardy said the team is interested in testing breath samples from children with cystic fibrosis. Persistent lung infections that involve biofilms can develop in these children.

Pseudomonas is a major cause of lung infections in people with the disease, according to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.

Custom electrodes are also being developed so that enough data can be collected from a single locust.

In the long term, the researchers want to build a portable sensor. It would connect a living locust’s smell system to small electronics and artificial intelligence.

More bacterial species and samples from patients will be needed in future work. The results will also have to be compared with the laboratory methods already used in hospitals.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

#6355. Eagles may hunt baboons as heavy as some early human relatives

Punctured baboon skulls found beneath cliffs in Chad suggest Verreaux’s eagles may hunt larger primates than scientists once thought possible.

Eagles are known to kill monkeys. A full-grown male baboon, however, has long been considered too heavy for any bird to take.

That view is now challenged by skulls of adult male olive baboons found below desert cliffs in the Sahara. The damage on them suggests that Verreaux’s eagles can kill such animals anyway.

A hole was punched through the bone of the eye socket in each skull. It is the kind of wound that an eagle’s talon leaves. One of the baboons weighed an estimated 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

If the researchers are right, an eagle can kill prey as heavy as some early human relatives.

The study was led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St Andrews. She worked with colleagues at Dartmouth College, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

No one on the team saw an eagle attack a baboon. The case rests on bones.

Three sites on the Ennedi Plateau were visited by the team in February and March 2025. The plateau is a sandstone landscape in northeastern Chad.

Among the fallen rock below its cliffs, the skulls of two adult male baboons were found at two different sites.

Neither puncture showed signs of healing, so the damage could have occurred around the time of death or afterward.

“We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Hobaiter said.

“Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”

The right shoulder blade of the first male had been punctured and scraped as well. Eagles leave that pattern when they open a body to reach the heart and lungs.

The team also needed to know how heavy the baboons were. The ball at the top of each thigh bone was therefore measured in scaled photographs.

An established formula for monkeys converts that width into an estimate of body weight.

Both thigh bones were found with the first punctured skull. From them, the team estimated that male’s weight at about 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

These weights matter because of a rule of thumb in research on primates and their predators. Primates under 29 pounds (13 kg) are known eagle prey. No heavier primate has ever been confirmed as an eagle’s kill.

Primates between 29 and 44 pounds (13 and 20 kg) are treated as vulnerable in theory. Anything heavier is assumed to be safe from birds.

A third punctured skull was recovered on a return trip in June 2026, along with part of the skeleton. This male weighed an estimated 58 pounds (26.2 kg), and both of his shoulder blades had been scraped.

He was at least twice as heavy as any primate confirmed as eagle prey.

In all, thigh bones were collected from nine baboons. Eight were adult males with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kg).

A hole in a baboon’s skull does not have to come from an eagle. Other causes were therefore considered by the team.

A gunshot would be expected to do much more damage to the skull, and none was found. Male baboons also kill each other with their canine teeth. Such fights tend to leave crushed bone and extra tooth gouges, yet the skulls had neither.

Verreaux’s eagles are known to dive at baboons that come near their nests. No nest was found above or near the skulls, however.

One possibility was harder to dismiss. Verreaux’s eagles sometimes eat dead animals. The scraped shoulder blade could be explained by an eagle pulling apart a carcass.

The authors wrote that this cannot be definitively ruled out. Two reasons to doubt it were given.

First, the skull punctures are far more severe than the shallow pits seen in an earlier experiment. In that experiment, a golden eagle had gripped a dead monkey.

Second, nearly all the bones came from adult males. An eagle that feeds on carcasses would be expected to eat a dead baboon of either sex.

“At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t,” said Nathaniel Dominy of Dartmouth, the study’s senior author.

An eagle does not have to lift its prey to kill it. Golden eagles land on the back of a hoofed animal and hold on until it collapses. Similar methods are used by Verreaux’s eagles.

Verreaux’s eagles also hunt in pairs. The prey is startled by one bird, and the other attacks from below to force it off the cliff.

The grip of a Verreaux’s eagle can span up to 16 inches (40 cm). That is more than twice the width of an adult male baboon’s skull.

The Ennedi baboons appear to spend much of the day on vertical cliff faces. Some are as tall as 490 feet (150 meters).

Water and palm fruit are found on the canyon floor, but it offers little shade or shelter.

When young baboons are threatened by an eagle, the males bark and lunge at it. The team suggested that this could make males more likely to be killed on a cliff.

On June 19, 2026, the researchers watched a pair of Verreaux’s eagles.

The birds flew along a cliff where baboons were resting. Several baboons gave alarm calls, and those in exposed spots dropped quickly to shelter.

“We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety,” Hobaiter said.

The argument reaches past baboons because of a famous fossil. In 1995, researchers argued that the Taung Child had been killed by an eagle.

The Taung Child was a young early human relative.

The punctures in the Ennedi skulls resemble the damage to that fossil’s eye socket. The Taung Child, however, weighed an estimated 22 to 26 pounds (10 to 12 kg) at most.

That weight falls inside the accepted limit for eagle prey.

Research on what hunted larger early human relatives has focused on mammals, especially big cats. Hobaiter’s team argued that eagles deserve attention too.

If eagles can kill adult baboons this large, the authors argue that some early human relatives may also have been vulnerable.

Monkeys defend themselves differently against eagles than against cats, and males often step in during eagle attacks.

Several traits could have been shaped by pressure from eagles, the authors wrote. These include the size difference between males and females, cooperation among males, and infant care.

That part of the argument was called speculative by the authors.

Three punctured skulls point to possible eagle attacks, and baboons sounded alarm calls when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles flew past.

The researchers have yet to see one of these eagles attack an adult baboon.

Nearly all the bones came from adult males, and the authors called that pattern puzzling.

3D scans of the bones have been posted in public archives by the researchers, where others can examine the punctures.

Future fieldwork at Ennedi could show whether eagles kill adult male baboons there, and how often.

The full study was published in the journal American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

#6354. Thanksgiving food waste can start before the turkey even goes in the oven

Americans wasted about 166,000 metric tons of food during Thanksgiving week in 2025, roughly 39% more than during a comparison week.

When Thanksgiving food waste comes up, leftovers usually get the blame.

The stuffing went unfinished, or half a pie stayed on the counter until Sunday. In some homes, though, good food is discarded before the meal is even cooked. It is thrown out so a shelf can be cleared for the turkey.

Researchers documented this habit in surveys of U.S. households around Thanksgiving 2025. More edible food was discarded by those households in the holiday week than in a later, ordinary week.

Extra waste was reported by cooks who emptied the fridge to make room. Cooks who had to guess their guests’ appetites reported more too, compared with cooks who made just enough.

The researchers therefore see the days before the meal as a chance to cut holiday waste.

Ran Li of Penn State University and Brian Roe of Ohio State University carried out the surveys. Roe is a professor of agricultural, environmental and development economics.

All of the figures are based on people’s own reports about their kitchens. Nobody’s trash was actually weighed.

“There’s not a lot of great data out there about which holidays cause the most waste,” Roe said. “My money would be on Thanksgiving because it is so focused around the meal – it is the big tradition.”

Household waste surveys normally skip holiday weeks, since researchers are after a typical week. Yearly totals based on such surveys therefore miss the holidays.

For this study, 879 adults were surveyed before and after Thanksgiving 2025. Every one of them handled at least half of the cooking at home.

About a week after the first survey, they reported how much food their households had not eaten. That included anything thrown out, composted or fed to pets.

Bones, peels and pits were left out of the count. Only once-edible food was included.

Later, in December, 437 of the same households repeated the exercise for a non-holiday week.

Households that reported in both weeks discarded about 1.1 pounds (500 grams) of edible food per person during Thanksgiving week.

About 0.8 pounds (358 grams) was discarded in the December week. The Thanksgiving total was therefore 39% higher.

People who skipped the holiday meal discarded about the same amount in both weeks.

The results were then scaled up to the whole country. By the authors’ estimate, Americans discarded about 367 million pounds (166,000 metric tons) of edible food during Thanksgiving week.

That amounts to roughly a pound for every person in the United States.

Based on respondents’ estimates, Americans wasted about $3 billion worth of edible food during Thanksgiving week, roughly 40% more than during the December comparison week.

“That’s a pretty healthy chunk of change, particularly as people are concerned about high food prices right now,” Roe said.

Four out of five respondents took part in a Thanksgiving meal as a host, a guest or both.

About 0.8 pounds (356 grams) per person was discarded that week by people who neither hosted nor attended a meal.

Guests who did not host averaged 1.2 pounds (545 grams). Hosts who did not attend another meal averaged 1.1 pounds (493 grams).

The highest average, 1.8 pounds (818 grams), was reported by respondents who hosted one meal and attended another. That is more than double the amount for people who skipped the holiday.

These gaps remained after age, income, household size and shopping habits were taken into account.

The meal was not blamed for all of that week’s waste. About a quarter of the discarded food was tied by respondents to hosting or attending a Thanksgiving meal.

Different foods were also thrown out by hosts and guests. More meat, turkey included, was discarded by hosts than by guests. Half of the people who only attended a meal had cooked a dish at home to bring.

About 500 respondents cooked for a Thanksgiving meal, either as hosts or as guests bringing a dish. Of those cooks, 74% said they had deliberately made more food than was needed.

The cooks gave three main reasons. Leftovers were the goal for the largest group, 37% of the cooks. Another 25% did not know how much their guests would eat. A further 12% said a big spread was the tradition.

Each of these groups reported more waste than cooks who tried to make just enough. Leftover planners reported about 0.4 pounds (189 grams) more per person for the week.

Cooks who were unsure reported about 0.8 pounds (363 grams) more.

A plan for the extra food was thus associated with less waste than a guess was.

For cooks who guess, tools such as the Guest-Imator were suggested by Li and Roe. It is a calculator from the Natural Resources Defense Council.

A guest count and the amount of leftovers wanted are entered, and the calculator returns quantities to buy.

A use for the extra food was found by many cooks. Among hosts, 37% sent guests home with leftovers. About one in six respondents with leftovers froze some.

The cooks were also asked about the days before the meal. Had food been thrown away to make room for the turkey and the other holiday groceries?

Nearly a pound (438 grams) more waste per person was reported for the week by cooks who cleared space. The comparison was with meal participants who neither cleared space nor cooked too much.

That extra amount alone exceeds the 0.8 pounds reported for the whole week by a person who skipped Thanksgiving.

“They would clear out a bunch of stuff,” Roe said.

Li and Roe wrote that campaigns before the holiday could help. One example they gave was recipes that use up fridge items the night before the turkey is bought.

“Think about what’s in the fridge that can be used up before the turkey’s coming in so that you can have that place for all your fixings for the holiday meal,” he said.

Respondents also reported where the food went: the trash, the compost or the sink.

During Thanksgiving week, 98% more food per person went down the sink or garbage disposal than in December.

Residents of some cities are warned around the holidays about fatbergs. These are buildups of fat, oil and grease that can damage sewer pipes.

The kind of food that went down the drain was not recorded. However, 85% more meat and fish was discarded during Thanksgiving week by households that reported in both weeks.

Li and Roe suspect that holiday cooking adds fat, oil and grease to what goes down the sink.

Because the study is a survey, it shows which habits were associated with more waste. It cannot show that any single habit caused the waste.

The respondents were drawn from an online research panel. Their answers were adjusted to match U.S. households on age, income and household size. Even so, the respondents were not a random sample.

In earlier research, surveys of this kind found 32% to 52% less waste than physical measurement of household waste did. The national totals may therefore be underestimates.

Each household’s waste was also divided by the number of people who normally live there. The number of people at the table was not used. A host’s figure therefore looks bigger, and a guest’s figure looks smaller.

Only about half of the Thanksgiving respondents reported again in December.

For some of them, the December week ended just before Christmas. That week may not have been an ordinary one either.

The survey also did not test any solution. It remains unknown if a portion calculator or a night of use-it-up cooking reduces what is thrown out.

According to Li and Roe, household waste should be weighed over a holiday in future studies.

They also recommended that similar surveys be run for other food-centered holidays.

The full study was published in the journal Waste.

Biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas lifts the lid on the secret life of tardigrades in stunning detail for the Nikon Small World photography awards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail.

In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition, a tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin.

"A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email.

"An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. The exuvium can therefore provide an additional layer of physical protection for the developing embryos."

In some species, males may place sperm inside the cuticle of a molting female before egg laying, according to National Geographic. In others, the males fertilize the eggs after they have been left inside the cuticle. And some don't even need males to reproduce at all.

"Many species reproduce through parthenogenesis," Quiroga-Artigas said, which is when an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, also known as a virgin birth. "This means that males are not required for reproduction, and the resulting offspring are genetically very similar to their mothers," he added. The species in the photograph falls into this category.

Molting and egg laying often take place over several hours, but the shedding itself is a relatively fast process. Capturing it on camera is, therefore, no mean feat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once I had collected animals that were laying eggs, I had to fix, stain, and mount the specimens before imaging them," Quiroga-Artigas said. "I then spent a long microscopy session searching for the right specimen and the right orientation to obtain a high-quality image. Finding a specimen at exactly the right stage of molting, and in an orientation that allows the process to be clearly visualized, is largely a matter of patience and luck."

—Tardigrades survive being dried out thanks to proteins found in no other animals on Earth

—Tardigrades may hitchhike on snails ... and then suffocate in their slime

—'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards

Photographing these animals is also challenging due to their tiny size. "Working with tardigrades in the lab requires a lot of experience with micromanipulation, as they are extremely small," Quiroga-Artigas said. "Hypsibius exemplaris, for example, is only about 250 µm [micrometers] long." That's about twice the width of a human hair.

This particular photo was taken using confocal microscopy, which uses a focused laser beam to light up one section at a time to create a detailed, high-resolution image. Quiroga-Artigas used this technique for a second tardigrade photo that was listed as an Image of Distinction in the same competition.

The second image submitted by Quiroga-Artigas to the Nikon Small World competition of a tardigrade shown from beneath.

He also received an Honorable Mention in the Nikon Small World in Motion Competition for a video of a pregnant tardigrade making contact with another tardigrade, which can then be seen pooping. However, it's not clear whether the contact between the two individuals caused this movement, Quiroga-Artigas said.

Quiroga-Artigas hopes his photography and videos give viewers an idea of just how beautiful and complex the microscopic world really is. "There are tiny animals all around us that we cannot see with the naked eye, yet they live, reproduce, grow, and undergo complex life cycles just like the animals we are more familiar with," he said.

"I will continue capturing images of tardigrades in different contexts related to my future research, without necessarily having a specific photographic goal in mind," he added. "In my experience, some of the best images I have captured were not necessarily the ones I was actively looking for."

Pandora is the trending news editor at Live Science. She is also a science presenter and previously worked as Senior Science and Health Reporter at Newsweek. Pandora holds a Biological Sciences degree from the University of Oxford, where she specialised in biochemistry and molecular biology.

#6352. Offshore wind turbines may reshape the low clouds around them

Clouds can change how much electricity offshore wind farms produce, while turbines can also thin low clouds nearby.

Low clouds over the sea do more than just block sunlight. The tops of these clouds lose heat to space, which cools the air and keeps it moving.

This moving air also affects the wind turbines below.

In computer simulations, turbines in the last rows produced about 11% more power when the air above the clouds was drier than when it was moister.

The wind turbines also affected the clouds. When the clouds were low enough to touch the turbine blades, the turbines made them thinner over several miles in the direction of the wind.

Clouds are left out of many simulations of offshore wind farms.

Researchers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands put them in. Their results suggest that planners of large offshore farms should take clouds into account.

All of this was tested in computer simulations, not at real wind farms.

The clouds in question are stratocumulus. These low, lumpy sheets are the most common cloud type on Earth.

In an average year, they cover about 25% to 30% of the North Sea. Wind energy projects are widespread there, and more are planned.

The North Sea is cloudy so often that its wind farms’ energy output may be affected, said Davide Selvatici. Selvatici is a postdoctoral researcher in the university’s Physics of Fluids group.

Modelers had often worked with idealized skies that held almost no cloud, said Richard Stevens. Stevens is a professor of fluid mechanics at Twente.

Thijs van den Ham, a co-author, said wind farm simulations need clouds in them. “They do play a role, and they do matter,” the author added.

Humidity by itself doesn’t do much to a turbine. Moist air and dry air differ in density by less than 1%. Power output changes by about the same amount.

So the team looked at how clouds change the air’s motion. An earlier study by Selvatici and Stevens had already examined this. In that work, the slowed wind behind a simulated farm recovered faster under low clouds.

The simulations were detailed enough to follow individual gusts and swirls of air.

The work was done in two stages. Cloud layers were first simulated without any turbines, and the temperature and moisture of the overlying air were varied. About 300 simulated hours passed before each of those layers reached a steady state.

A wind farm was then added beneath a selection of those cloud layers. It had 60 turbines in 10 staggered rows, and each was rated at 10 megawatts.

Rotors measured 585 feet (178 meters) across, which put the blade tips 682 feet (208 meters) above the water.

The Washington Monument is shorter than that. At such a height, the blades could reach into the lowest simulated clouds.

A block of air 37 miles (60 kilometers) long surrounded the farm in the model. The block was divided into more than 560 million cells.

Two sets of runs were carried out so that the cloud’s effect could be separated from the effect of moisture.

Cooling at the cloud top was held fixed in the first set. In the second set, cooling was allowed to respond to the moisture overhead, which is how real clouds behave.

When cooling was held fixed, the drier and moister cases differed by about 3% in power from the last rows. A gap that small lies within the uncertainty of the simulations.

Once cooling was allowed to respond, the same comparison produced a difference of 11%.

The cloud itself was responsible for the larger difference, according to the team’s analysis.

Heat is emitted upward by a cloud top, while water vapor in the overlying air radiates heat back down. Less heat is returned by drier air, so the top of the cloud cools more quickly.

That stronger cooling stirred the air underneath more vigorously and the cloud-topped layer deepened. As a result, more of the wind’s energy was transported downward into the farm.

Energy arriving from above is most important at the back of a wind farm.

More than half of the power in the front rows comes from wind that flows in. Each row, however, leaves slower air in its wake for the rows that follow.

In the final rows of the simulated farm, turbulent mixing supplied up to about 90% of a row’s power.

A second effect appeared when the air above the cloud was moister. The cloud-topped layer was then shallower and the approaching wind was slowed more strongly ahead of the farm. The first row of turbines produced less power as a consequence.

Temperature was also found to matter. In the runs with fixed cooling, the researchers varied the temperature contrast between the sea surface and the air above.

The air temperature was taken about 2 miles (3 kilometers) up. The farm’s output then differed by about 20% from a reference case.

Satellite images had already suggested that wind farms affect clouds.

On two mornings, June 5, 2016, and November 14, 2022, North Sea wind farms were photographed by NASA’s Terra satellite. The images showed partly cleared cloud near clusters of wind farms. The team took them from NASA Worldview.

The simulated thinning was strongest under two conditions. The base of the cloud was near the blade tips, and the cloud held little liquid water.

In the run with the lowest cloud, the cloud layer’s top was 587 feet (179 meters) above the sea. That is below the blade tips.

Behind the farm, that cloud held up to 85% less liquid water than in a matching run without turbines.

Warmer, drier air from above was mixed into the cloud by turbulence from the turbines. More of the cloud’s water evaporated.

Ahead of the farm, the cloud changed the opposite way.

The wind slowed as it approached the first row. In that same run, the cloud there held up to about 43% more liquid water than the incoming cloud.

The authors compared that to the Horns Rev wind farm. There, slowing wind ahead of the turbines has been linked to fog forming upwind.

Every run was set in the daytime, with the sun at a fixed angle. Sunlight weakens a low cloud, and the authors wrote that daytime conditions may have amplified the thinning.

The simulations also had no rain, a single farm layout, and the same large-scale wind in every run.

The simulated clouds thinned in the same general way as the photographed ones. The amounts were not compared.

Large clusters of wind farms weren’t simulated either. The authors wrote that those need more observations and more modeling.

Next, the team plans to simulate more kinds of weather and larger farms spaced farther apart. Selvatici noted that simulating real weather conditions will take more computing power than is available now.

The full study was published in the Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy.

#6351. Even powdery mildew can catch a fungal infection

Researchers found a fungus that infects powdery mildew in preserved specimens, offering clues to how it might help control the crop disease.

Powdery mildew is usually the one doing the damage. The fungi behind it infect crops such as wheat and grapevines, yet some of those mildews are infected themselves, by a fungus called Ampelomyces that lives inside their cells.

Researchers checked dried mildew specimens up to about 150 years old and found the parasite on mildews from many countries.

The study also found that about 13% of the public DNA records labeled Ampelomyces appear to belong to other fungi.

Michael Bradshaw, an assistant professor of entomology and plant pathology at North Carolina State University, led the research with first author Jacklyn Thomas.

Bradshaw directs the university’s Larry F. Grand Mycological Herbarium.

He sees the parasite as a possible tool against the disease. Part of the reason is host specificity, meaning some strains infect only certain kinds of mildew.

“By understanding hyperparasite diversity and how many different strains are out there, it might give us insights on if some are better at controlling the fungus than others,” Bradshaw said.

“There is a degree of host specificity to these hyperparasites, and if we are able to delve deeper they may be very useful in containing this plant disease.”

Powdery mildews include more than 900 species. Together they cause disease in more than 10,000 kinds of flowering plants.

Powdery mildew fungi need living plant tissue to grow, so scientists can’t grow them in lab cultures. That makes their parasite hard to study as well.

So the team turned to herbaria, collections of preserved plants and fungi. The researchers screened 609 mildew specimens held at North Carolina State and at Harvard University’s Farlow Herbarium.

The specimens came from 28 countries, from Argentina and Morocco to Japan and Ukraine. Many reached North Carolina as gifts from herbaria in Germany and Japan.

From each specimen, the team scraped a bit of mildew and tested its DNA for the parasite.

The researchers then checked every positive result under a microscope.

Researchers lifted the mildew onto clear tape and found Ampelomyces under a microscope.

Ampelomyces turned up in 40 of the 609 specimens, or 6.6%. The authors wrote that old collections let them detect a parasite that is hard to observe directly.

Some kinds of mildew were infected far more often than others. Sawadaea mildews had the highest rate, at 14.3%.

Podosphaera and Phyllactinia mildews were among the lowest, at 3.2% and 2.7%.

Some of those groups had only a few specimens, the authors wrote, so small samples may explain part of the spread.

Researchers in Serbia and Hungary, examining field samples under a microscope, had found the parasite in about a third of them.

The detection rate in the herbarium specimens was much lower.

The authors suggested reasons for the gap. Their samples came from many parts of the world, and their DNA tests could miss strains whose genetic code differed from what the tests were built to match.

The team sorted its strains, along with hundreds from public records, by how closely related they were.

Strains from Podosphaera mildews tended to group together, and so did strains from a genus called Arthrocladiella.

Strains from Erysiphe, the largest mildew genus, were scattered across many groups.

The mix of tight groups and scattered strains suggests some Ampelomyces lineages specialize while others infect many kinds of mildew.

Several strains from the herbarium specimens matched no known group and may be new lineages.

One specimen of a mildew called Blumeria showed the parasite under the microscope, but its DNA test failed. The authors suggested that Ampelomyces on Blumeria may be a lineage not yet described.

GenBank is a public database where scientists share DNA sequences. The team downloaded all 671 sequences filed there as Ampelomyces and placed them in one family tree.

Of those sequences, 88 fell outside the main Ampelomyces branch. That is how the team arrived at its estimate that about 13% were probably other fungi.

Even samples from culture collections, which supply living strains to labs, were mislabeled.

One strain listed as Ampelomyces had DNA identical to a fungus called Didymella, though the authors wrote that it may have been contaminated after it left the collection.

Bradshaw said errors like these are a risk whenever researchers rely on large datasets that anyone can add to.

“These parasites are hard to identify, so what happens is someone misidentifies them and enters incorrect data,” he said.

“Then someone else sees that wrong data and uses it to classify their own samples, which leads to more wrong data, and it amplifies that way.”

The team’s answer is a checked reference tree of 47 confirmed strains, posted to a free online tool called T-BAS. Researchers can upload a sequence and see where it belongs.

There are limits. The family tree rests mostly on one short piece of DNA, and its main Ampelomyces branch was only weakly supported.

More genetic data will help sort out how the strains are related, the authors wrote.

Two big questions remain. Are some strains better at fighting the fungus than others?

And did the parasite and the mildew evolve together? Answering the second question will take more samples and whole genomes.

Future research could also expand sampling to more regions and more mildews.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings B.

#6349. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China are revealing that at least two lineages of early humans were present in the region around 184,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint.

The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo. The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there.

"I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science.

H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. It is one of the longest-surviving hominin species, and the last known record of it is from 108,000 years ago in river flood plains in Java, Indonesia. However, there was no physical evidence of H. erectus being on the Asian mainland more recently than 400,000 years ago.

But in two caves in Guangxi province in southern China, researchers have found thousands of mammalian fossils, accumulated there by porcupines that scavenged for and collected bones. The Baxian and Naxian caves are about 9 miles (15 kilometers) apart, sitting in a karst landscape of limestone formations that are prone to dissolving to create caves that would have offered crucial shelter for H. erectus.

The entrance to Naxian Cave, as seen by a drone, is the tall and wide opening of a cave that goes back around 330 feet (100 meters) to a fossil chamber.

Researchers found the nine human teeth among more than 18,000 fossils, including from apes, elephants, rhinoceroses and other ancient hoofed animals, Welker and his colleagues reported in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature.

Radiometric dating of the fossils and surrounding sediments by methods including assessing the decay of uranium, pins them to about 324,000 to 184,000 years ago. Eight of the teeth have physical features reminiscent of H. erectus, but the ninth is more elusive. It looks distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals and modern humans, Welker said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Welker's team took samples from five teeth ‪—‬ four from the group that seemed to be H. erectus and one from the mysterious tooth ‪—‬ to see which ancient proteins were present, since DNA tends to degrade more easily than the proteins in an organism. (The study of these proteins is known as proteomics.)

The four similar ones had protein signatures that matched what had been seen before in H. erectus.

"The morphology is nicely confirmed by the proteomics," Welker told Live Science. Three of these teeth were from males, and the other was from a female, which the team was able to determine based on the presence or absence of amelogenin-Y, a protein coded for only by the Y chromosome.

Researchers investigating two caves in China have found nine human teeth, eight of which have been confidently identified as belonging to Homo erectus.

However, some parts of the protein signatures differed from what had been seen in other H. erectus remains in China, so the new specimens may be from a previously unknown H. erectus population that perhaps had a slightly different genetic makeup, Welker said.

The finding that H. erectus was present in mainland Asia until at least 184,000 years ago — rather than 400,000 years ago — fills a geographical and chronological gap, helping to explain how H. erectus was on Java 108,000 years ago.

"This brings the history of H. erectus in East Asia closer in age to the late Javanese examples, raising the possibility that these populations were connected through land bridges at times of lowered sea level," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who wasn't involved in the study, previously believed that specimens from the past 400,000 years or so flagged as H. erectus were actually Denisovans ‪—‬ ancient humans who lived in Asia, disappeared around 30,000 years ago and belonged to the Homo longi lineage. But he told Live Science that the new morphological and protein findings provide convincing evidence that H. erectus did survive until relatively recently in some places.

The fifth analyzed tooth, known as PA1796, remains mysterious. The protein analysis revealed it was from a male, but it didn't show a recognizable signature in the protein sequence data. Therefore, Welker's team suggested it could be from another hominin species that was present in the region at the same time.

Welker didn’t want to speculate about which species it might be, but said: "Sequence-wise it doesn't have this Homo erectus substitution and morphologically, it doesn't look like an erectus tooth."

The tooth could be from a previously unknown human species, but many experts suspect it is from a Denisovan.

"With some of the new material probably dating to less than 200,000 years old, this already brings it close in age to known or putative Homo longi/Denisovan samples in southern China and Laos, implying potentially long overlaps between these species," Stringer said. "Tooth PA1796 could represent a longi/Denisovan, though it is relatively small in size, and relevant comparative data for longi/Denisovans is sparse."

The entrance to China's Naxian Cave, which has a small opening and goes back around 164 feet (50 m) to a fossil chamber.

Recent research suggests there was interbreeding between the H. erectus and Denisovan lineages, and the new evidence increases the likelihood that this happened, at least occasionally, Stringer said.

Any firm conclusions of who the tooth is from will have to wait for further finds of similar teeth elsewhere, Welker said.

Hawks agreed that the tooth is most likely from a Denisovan, perhaps from a divergent branch for which we don't have protein data. But it could also be from a novel H. erectus population or someone from the same population as the other teeth who, for developmental or genetic reasons, wasn't typical. "I would have liked to see additional comparisons in the paper to more Denisovan teeth," Hawks said.

In another paper, also published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature, Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, and her colleagues examined trace elements in the same teeth, as well as in animal teeth from the caves, to see what they revealed about the hominins' diet and local habitat.

Their analysis indicated that this H. erectus population found plants and animals to eat in tropical, rainforest-like ecosystems. Previously, it was thought that only our own species, Homo sapiens, was able to adapt to this type of environment.

"Rather than being confined to open woodland and grassland environments, H. erectus was considerably more ecologically adaptable than many of us have assumed," Stringer said.

"Being adaptable and being flexible are not traits that we associate with ancient human species — these are traits that we associate with H. sapiens," Westaway told Live Science. "Suddenly we're seeing H. erectus being able to survive in environments that we didn't think they could possibly survive in."

And given the mysterious tooth, it is possible that two different early human populations were this adaptable, said Welker, who was a co-author of the study.

A view from Naxian Cave in China, where Homo erectus teeth were found.

Westaway and her colleagues also looked at levels of the element strontium in the teeth, which can shed light on where someone grew up based on the unique strontium levels in water and foods they consumed as children. The team matched these strontium levels to another karst landscape about 200 miles (320 km) away, in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

"It looks like H. erectus moved across large areas, traversing this karst landscape in the rainforests" ‪—‬ a finding that adds to our understanding of these ancient humans, Westaway said.

It's absurd that people often think of H. erectus as an unsuccessful species, she added. "We think they were the first to leave Africa, the first to use fire. It blows my mind because they survived six times longer than H. sapiens has survived so far, so I don't see them as unsuccessful."

Hawks' big question, however, is linked to modern humans, who were in the Chinese region from at least 45,000 years ago.

"Denisovan DNA is present in the peoples of Island Southeast Asia, so, modern humans must have run into Denisovans at some point," he said. "If H. erectus was enduring in the same area at the same time, might H. sapiens also have encountered late H. erectus?"

#6347. The fossil fuel ‘carbon bubble’ may be smaller than investors once feared

A new study estimates a $99.3 billion carbon bubble among major U.S.-listed fossil fuel companies, with climate policy risks varying by company.

Major fossil-fuel companies may be overvalued by about $99.3 billion because of climate policy risks, according to new research.

That amounts to roughly 5.5% of the market value examined, suggesting investors have already priced in some of the transition.

Researchers at the University of Technology Sydney’s Centre for Climate Risk and Resilience worked with colleagues at Macquarie University.

They investigated how major climate policy developments affected the value of leading fossil-fuel companies listed in the United States.

The findings suggest a smaller potential correction than some earlier estimates. They also point to considerable differences in how individual companies might fare.

The carbon bubble describes a concern about what fossil-fuel businesses are really worth as the world moves toward cleaner energy.

Their valuations depend partly on future earnings from coal, oil and gas. Stronger climate policies or falling demand could reduce those earnings, leaving reserves undeveloped and infrastructure less valuable.

If investors underestimate those changes, share prices may be higher than future business prospects justify. A correction could then bring losses for shareholders and financial institutions.

The researchers set out to estimate that gap, while allowing for the possibility that markets already recognize some climate risks.

The team examined 31 major climate policy signals between 1996 and 2023.

These comprised 27 United Nations climate conferences and four significant announcements in the United States and European Union.

Using stock and options market information, they estimated company values under two scenarios.

One assumed business as usual without additional climate-policy constraints; the other incorporated climate-related policy risks.

The difference produced the estimated bubble of 5.5%, or $99.3 billion, for the largest US-listed fossil-fuel companies with traded options.

That figure concerns the companies studied. It does not measure the potential losses across every fossil-fuel business or project worldwide.

Nor does it predict an inevitable crash. The results suggest markets may be adjusting gradually, with some transition risks already reflected in prices.

“The findings challenge the assumption that stronger climate policies must automatically lead to substantial financial losses for every fossil-fuel company,” said lead researchers Mona Mashhadi Rajabi and Martina Linnenluecke from Sydney.

“Companies are not all equally exposed to the energy transition. Their financial position can depend on the quality of their assets, their investment decisions, their ability to adapt and how effectively they prepare for a changing energy market.”

“This is an important distinction. A company that recognizes transition risks early, adjusts its investment strategy and prepares for changes in energy demand may be better positioned than one that continues to rely on the assumption that current business conditions will last indefinitely.”

The sector-wide estimate therefore leaves an important question for investors: which businesses are preparing, and which are counting on little changing?

A relatively modest estimate does not remove the uncertainty surrounding future fossil fuel demand.

Projects that look profitable today may earn less under different policies or more competitive clean-energy alternatives.

Assets built to operate for decades are particularly exposed to those changes. Their economics depend on conditions well beyond the next reporting period.

“So, the key message of this research is not that fossil-fuel companies are financially safe. Significant transition risks remain, and these need to be assessed carefully. Importantly, risks will change as the stringency of carbon policies changes,” the scientists explained.

“For policymakers, the findings reinforce the importance of clear and predictable climate policies. For investors and financial institutions, the results are a reminder to look beyond headline estimates of stranded assets.”

Stranded assets are reserves or infrastructure that lose economic value before their expected useful life ends. Their potential scale matters, but it cannot alone explain how a whole company will perform.

Investment choices, asset quality, and the ability to change direction also influence future earnings. Assessing those differences requires information about how companies intend to respond.

“Climate-related financial disclosure can help investors distinguish between companies that are preparing for the transition and those that remain heavily exposed to changing market conditions,” the researchers said.

The research puts that distinction at the center of the debate. A single estimate of potential overvaluation cannot tell investors which projects will remain competitive or which strategies will work.

For Australia, the findings have implications beyond the stock market. Decisions about new fossil-fuel projects commit money to assets whose working lives may span substantial changes in overseas demand.

“These questions are particularly important for Australia, one of the world’s major exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas (LNG). The value of Australia’s fossil-fuel industries is closely connected to demand in international markets,” the authors wrote.

“Australia therefore needs to look beyond current export revenues when making decisions about future energy investment. A project that appears commercially attractive today may face a different economic outlook over its operating life.”

“Equally, assuming that all fossil-fuel assets will rapidly lose value could lead to decisions that overlook differences in project economics and market exposure.”

“The carbon bubble debate should move beyond predictions of a sudden collapse. What matters now is whether companies, investors and governments are making decisions that reflect the energy markets of the future, rather than relying solely on the conditions of the past.”

The study is published in the journal Sustainable Futures.

#6346. A vanished bird from Haiti may help solve an ancient Pacific mystery

DNA reveals how snipes and woodcocks reached distant islands, stopped migrating, changed physically, and became vulnerable to extinction.

The sandpiper family includes some of the most extreme long-distance migrants among birds.

Two branches of that family, the snipes and the woodcocks, have behaved quite differently. These birds reached islands again and again, and migration was then abandoned.

Nearly every living species was examined in a new DNA study.

The results suggest that island settlement was accompanied by changes in body size and flying ability. Island species later proved vulnerable when people arrived with rats and cats.

The work was led by Min Zhao, then a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. Colleagues at Virginia Tech and the Field Museum in Chicago also took part.

According to Zhao, the whole project grew out of one extinct bird from Hispaniola. That Caribbean island is shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

The dates reported in the study were estimated from family trees built with DNA. The uncertainty attached to them can run to millions of years.

Florida Museum researchers dug the bird’s bones out of a cave in Haiti in 1984.

In 2015, those bones were described by two scientists as a new species of woodcock. Woodcocks are long-billed birds that probe soft soil for food.

One of the two scientists was David Steadman, who is now an emeritus curator at the museum. He is also listed as a co-author of the new study.

Zhao’s team extracted DNA from two of the fossil specimens. The researchers then read the mitochondrial genome, a small set of genes passed from mother to offspring.

Both specimens were placed with the snipes, which form the sister group of the woodcocks. Their closest living relative turned out to be the giant snipe of lowland South America.

The analysis suggested a South American origin for the Haitian bird’s ancestors. The two lineages are thought to have split between 5 and 12 million years ago.

Why, then, did the bones resemble those of a woodcock? The authors think the bird’s build may have been altered by island living, which could explain the mix-up.

The outer wing bone of the Haitian bird was unusually short when compared with its upper wing bone. The authors wrote that it could fly but probably not well.

The team sequenced 45 samples in total. Two were the Haitian fossils and 19 were toe pads taken from old museum specimens. The remaining 24 were fresh tissue samples.

All but one of the 29 living species of snipes and woodcocks were covered by these samples. Specimens were supplied by ten museums and research collections.

A family tree was built from the data, and both groups were traced back to Eurasia.

The ancestors of today’s American birds crossed from the Eastern Hemisphere to the Western Hemisphere four separate times.

One of those crossings took place roughly 20 million years ago. It was then that the ancestor of the American woodcock reached North America.

The researchers could not tell whether the bird arrived across the Atlantic or by way of Alaska.

The Austral snipes are found on the outlying islands of New Zealand. Scientists have long placed these small brown birds in a group of their own.

Some snipes from Eurasia spend each winter in Australia and on nearby islands. The DNA showed that those visitors are not close relatives of the Austral snipes.

Instead, the Austral snipes share a branch with several large South American snipes and the extinct Haitian bird.

Two DNA datasets placed the split between the Austral snipes and their relatives at about 14 million and nearly 18 million years ago, respectively.

The southern continents had broken apart long before either estimate. The snipes’ ancestor most likely crossed the Pacific.

How the crossing happened remains an open question. The authors suggested that birds straying far outside their normal range may have played a role. Such straying was perhaps caused by extreme weather.

The authors also raised a route through Antarctica. Patches of treeless tundra are thought to have lasted there until at least 12.8 million years ago.

Several living snipe species still breed on tundra in the Arctic.

The analysis indicated that the ancestors of both snipes and woodcocks were migrants. Their island descendants are not.

Ten of the 29 living species are found only on islands, and none of those ten migrates.

The habit was lost several times. Woodcocks gave it up when they settled the Malay Archipelago in Southeast Asia. Snipes did the same when they settled South America and Madagascar.

Body size changed as well, although not in a single direction.

The Amami woodcock of southern Japan is about 45% heavier than the Eurasian woodcock, its closest mainland relative. Madagascar’s snipe is about 91% heavier than the common snipe of Eurasia.

The opposite change is seen in the Austral snipes. Their average weight is 3.4 ounces (96 grams), which is about the weight of a deck of cards.

South American snipes on the same branch average 8.6 ounces (243.5 grams). That is more than twice as much.

The smaller size may be explained by scarce food, the authors suggested. Competition from kiwis and other birds that probe the soil for worms was also considered possible.

Ten species of snipes and woodcocks are known to have died out in the recent geologic past. Nine of them lived on islands.

The Austral snipes suffered the heaviest losses. Three of nine known species survive. All three are ranked as Vulnerable or Near Threatened by the IUCN Red List.

The South Island snipe died out in 1964, and introduced black rats are regarded as the likely cause.

No resident snipe or woodcock is left in the Caribbean. At least three species have been lost there.

The youngest dated bones of the Haitian bird are about 600 years old. Rats and feral cats brought by people are suspected of causing its extinction.

Snipes nest on the ground, where they can be reached by those predators. Island species had given up migration, and in some cases strong flight as well.

The authors wrote that these changes made such species especially vulnerable to human impacts.

Overhunting was named as one of those impacts.

Jessica Oswald, a co-author, also worked on the study at the Florida Museum.

“People will eat anything,” said Oswald. She said a crew of hungry explorers or whalers could wipe out an island’s birds in a single weekend.

Island woodcocks in Japan and Southeast Asia appear to have fared better. They live in mountain forests, which may be harder for people to reach.

New Zealand may have been reached first by the Austral snipes.

From there they could have spread to Norfolk Island, New Caledonia and Fiji. The opposite path cannot be ruled out, because no genetic data exist for those islands’ extinct snipes.

More snipe species may once have lived in the Pacific and are now extinct. In that case, today’s birds would be the last survivors of a larger group. Direct fossil evidence of that link across the Pacific is still missing.

The Haitian bird’s place on the tree rests on mitochondrial genes from two specimens. A possible close relative from Puerto Rico is also extinct and has not been tested genetically.

The authors suggest that DNA from fossils yet to be found on Pacific islands could help trace how snipes spread across the region.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6345. Could Earth have been collecting dark matter for billions of years?

Heat measurements from dead stars helped physicists narrow down how dark matter might interact with ordinary matter.

Physicists have spent decades building dark matter detectors deep underground, and they still haven’t caught a single particle.

A new study suggests that Earth itself, along with the Sun, Jupiter and a handful of dead stars, might trap certain kinds of dark matter better than any lab instrument.

These bodies could have been collecting slow-moving particles for billions of years.

The researchers used neutrino data and heat measurements to rule out some combinations of particle mass and interaction strength that laboratory experiments couldn’t probe.

The work was led by Alejandro Ibarra from the Technical University of Munich, Merlin Reichard from the Korea Institute for Advanced Study and Gaurav Tomar from the Sogang University in Seoul.

About 85% of the matter in the universe is dark matter. We know it’s there because galaxies spin faster than their visible matter can explain and light bends more than it should as it passes them.

Beyond that, very little is known about it. Physicists are stuck in a frustrating loop.

You can’t identify something you can’t see, and you can’t design a way to see it without some idea of what it is. So they make a guess, build an experiment to test it, and so far the answer has always been no.

One guess is that dark matter isn’t completely dark. Its particles might respond to electricity and magnetism very faintly, carrying a tiny fraction of an electron’s charge or acting like microscopic magnets.

The paper describes five such properties. One of them, the “anapole moment,” is a doughnut-shaped kind of magnetism.

Any of the five would let a dark matter particle occasionally bump into an atom.

Underground detectors wait for those bumps. A slow particle taps an atom so gently that the instrument doesn’t notice.

In practice, these detectors are more sensitive to faster dark matter particles.

Planets and stars work the other way around. A fast particle shoots straight through them. A slow one only needs to lose a little speed in a collision before gravity grabs it and won’t let go.

Over billions of years, trapped particles would sink toward the center and crowd together. Once packed tightly enough, they could meet and annihilate, turning into other particles.

Some of those would be neutrinos, which pass through rock almost as if it weren’t there. The rest would deposit their energy as heat.

“In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” Tomar said.

“There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”

For the Sun and Earth, the team used limits from IceCube, a detector built into the Antarctic ice, and from its smaller companion detector, DeepCore.

That included ten years of IceCube data on neutrinos coming from Earth’s core. There was no excess.

Neither Jupiter nor the white dwarfs generate heat through nuclear fusion.

The Cassini spacecraft measured how much heat Jupiter leaks from its interior.

The white dwarfs are burnt-out stellar cores in M4, a cluster of ancient stars. Each one holds about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass in a ball with a radius of roughly 1,250 kilometers.

If a candidate type of dark matter would make these objects give off more heat than they actually do, it can be crossed off.

Earth turned out to be the best test for dark matter with a tiny electric charge. For particles heavier than about ten protons, it set the strongest limits yet.

There are two reasons. First, a charged particle’s pull reaches a long way, so it is easily drawn in. Second, Earth’s core is full of iron, whose atoms each carry 26 protons, which makes collisions more likely.

The white dwarfs set leading limits on two of the more exotic properties, the charge radius and the anapole moment, across a wide range of particle masses.

For very heavy particles, they also beat earlier limits on dark matter’s magnetic dipole moment.

The anapole limits matter for one popular candidate whose only possible electromagnetic property is the anapole moment.

For that candidate, the white dwarfs reach places that particle colliders and underground detectors struggle to get to.

Jupiter was a letdown. In general, it didn’t improve on limits that already existed. None of the four bodies beat earlier limits on the electric dipole moment either.

Underground labs sit beneath a kilometer or more of rock to block cosmic rays. If dark matter interacts strongly with ordinary matter, that same rock could slow it down or stop it before it reaches the detector.

The shield could be hiding the very particles the experiment is looking for.

Planets and stars don’t have this problem. The more strongly dark matter interacts, the better they catch it.

There is one important caveat. The more dark matter surrounds a star, the more of it the star can capture, and nobody has measured how much dark matter M4 contains.

The team had to rely on estimates from models.

“We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar noted.

Tomar suggests two places to look next. One is even colder white dwarfs in regions with more dark matter, where any extra heat would be easier to detect.

The other is beyond the Solar System, where exoplanets could serve as dark matter traps too.

The study is published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.
