Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence.

Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental.

But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes, quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper?

"You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science.

For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible.

In Einstein's general theory of relativity, matter and energy bend space-time and we experience that curvature as gravity. Quantum mechanics, meanwhile, describes nature on the smallest scales of atoms and subatomic particles.

But quantum mechanics still has no adequate description of the force of gravity. The conflict between these theories of big and small becomes unavoidable in extreme environments, such as the centers of black holes or the smallest fractions of a second after the Big Bang, where gravity grows to be intense on the minute scales ruled by quantum mechanics.

An artist's illustration of the Big Bang with time running from the image's bottom to the top. During the first brief fraction of a second after the Big Bang the universe was so dense that quantum effects and gravity were equally strong.

So far, efforts to combine them mathematically and theoretically have led to nonsensical results.

"They seem not to fit together into a single, consistent framework that we know to be correct," Latham Boyle, a theoretical physicist at the University of Edinburgh in the U.K, told Live Science.

It's possible that one or both of these theories is incomplete, but an increasingly popular belief among physicists is that both theories are perched upon an untested assumption: space-time itself.

Both general relativity and quantum mechanics assume that space-time exists. Yet neither explains why our universe seems to have three dimensions of space and one of time, or where space-time comes from. If this assumption is wrong, the apparent foundation of reality could be a large-scale approximation of something even more mysterious.

In Einstein's model, space-time is a little like how people once viewed water: smooth and continuous, capable of bending and rippling. But water only appears continuous on large scales because we can't see its composite "bits," or individual molecules, said Boyle, whose research explores quantum gravity, the early universe and whether space-time is fundamental or emergent. One proposal is that space-time is similar.

"It seems smooth but only because we can't view it under a fine enough microscope," Boyle told Live Science. Yet no one has found direct evidence for space-time's microscopic "bits." That leaves physicists searching for indirect clues in places where existing theories are pushed to their breaking point: black holes.

At the hearts of black holes, general relativity breaks down by predicting space-time curving infinitely, while quantum physics gives their boundaries baffling properties.

Around black holes gravity (the curvature of space-time) is warped to an infinite degree.

Black holes also offer intriguing clues that space-time, like water, may have microscopic ingredients. One clue comes from thermodynamics ‪—‬ the laws governing heat, temperature and entropy.

Entropy is often described as measuring the disorder in a system, but physicists use it to describe how many hidden microscopic arrangements can produce the same large-scale behavior. A glass of water, for example, may have one temperature and pressure even though its molecules could be moving and arranged in an enormous number of different ways. The more possible microscopic arrangements there are, the greater its entropy.

This matters because thermodynamics usually describes the large-scale behavior of microscopic ingredients. If Einstein’s equations are thermodynamic in nature, their entropy may be due to hidden microscopic states of space-time that physicists cannot yet see.

"General relativity is thermodynamics," Forshaw said. "Einstein's equations are a statement of thermodynamics. They're a statistically emergent feature of an underlying theory."

In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that black holes, too, have entropy and a physical temperature. This raised striking questions: Are there microscopic ingredients that account for those thermodynamic properties, and if so, what are they?

If those constituents exist, then space-time's smooth geometry, like the continuous appearance of water, emerges only on larger scales.

Another clue is that Einstein's equations appear to contain traces of this hidden structure, somehow reproducing the relationships needed for black holes to have a temperature, even though the theory directly connects the shape of space-time only to the matter it contains.

"Einstein's equation, which we thought was just a classical equation, nothing to do with quantum mechanics, seems to secretly know — or at some level to have known — about this finite entropy associated with the black hole," Boyle said.

The entropy of black holes also gives rise to a second sign that space-time emerges from something deeper: a puzzle known as the black hole information paradox.

Stephen Hawking in front of a projection of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula for black holes.

Quantum mechanics says that physical information can never be destroyed. Yet if black holes emit radiation — an idea famously proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1974 — they should slowly evaporate. This is a profound contradiction: A black hole's Hawking radiation is thermal, depending solely on its mass, electric charge and angular momentum. It contains no obvious record of what originally fell inside. That means that if the black hole eventually disappears, the information of what it once gobbled up seems to vanish with it.

But a black hole's entropy scales not with the three-dimensional volume enclosed by it but with the two-dimensional area of its event horizon, the point beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Therefore, it's possible that all the information within any region might somehow be stored on its boundary. This became known as the holographic principle, named after a hologram, in which a 3D image is encoded on a 2D surface.

In 1997, theoretical physicist Juan Maldacena made the idea mathematically precise. He showed that a higher-dimensional theory containing gravity could be mapped onto a lower-dimensional quantum theory without it.

The two descriptions appeared to be interchangeable, equally valid views of reality. But some researchers now go further: They think the lower-dimensional quantum theory may be the fundamental description, while the higher-dimensional space-time we seem to live in is what emerges when its information is decoded.

These ideas gave rise to holography. Its central principle is that a gravitational world in more dimensions may be completely encoded by a quantum theory without gravity in fewer dimensions. That lower-dimensional theory lives on the boundary of the higher-dimensional spacetime.

You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real

Mark Van Raamsdonk, a professor of physics at the University of British Columbia, compares the concept to a computer's memory chip. At the fundamental level, a video game is encoded in physical bits switching between states. Yet on a screen, those bits produce a representation of a 3D world containing objects, movement and physical rules. The virtual world seems spatially real, even though its underlying information is stored very differently.

"You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real," Van Raamsdonk told Live Science.

Quantum entanglement may play a central role in how this lower-dimensional information gives rise to higher-dimensional space-time. It describes how particles can share linked quantum properties, even when separated by vast distances.

"If I want to decode what space-time geometry is being stored by the quantum state of this lower-dimensional system, all I need to do is probe this entanglement structure," Van Raamsdonk said.

For decades, directly testing this theory appeared hopeless. Physicists thought they would need particle collisions approaching the Planck scale — the fantastically high energy at which quantum effects are expected to become as important as gravity, and far beyond anything existing colliders can produce.

But physicists realized they don't need to rely on brute force. They are now developing several ways around that energy barrier.

The CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Reaching the Planck scale requires roughly 900 trillion times more energy than the Large Hadron Collider can produce.

How could scientists discover whether space-time has a deeper structure? One way is to search for a subtle jitter, or static hum, in space-time itself. Experiments such as GQuEST, a collaboration involving Fermilab and Caltech, and QUEST at Cardiff University in the U.K. split laser light along different paths and recombine it. Extraordinarily small changes in the distance light travels may reveal fluctuations, arising from discrete building blocks of space-time, that are consistent with some of holography's models.

In some holographic models, physicists represent the underlying units of information as quantum bits (qubits) — mathematically identical to those used in quantum computers. Physically, a computer qubit may be encoded in an ion or electrical circuit, whereas a qubit in a holographic model represents a possible microscopic unit of the quantum theory from which space-time emerges. This equivalence allows quantum processors to simulate space-time models.

In such models, the patterns of entanglement between the qubits dictate the physical distances between regions of space. The stronger those entanglements are, the closer together two corresponding regions are; if the entanglements are severed, the space-time between them tears apart.

QUEST compares measurements from two neighboring laser beam splitters, or interferometers. Some theoretical models predict quantum fluctuations of space-time that would affect both instruments in a related way. Researchers therefore search for matching fluctuations in their measurements while working to rule out shared sources of laboratory noise. Finding the predicted pattern could support those models; finding nothing would constrain how strong such fluctuations could be, killing off flawed models and refining how microscopic components (or chunks of information) translate into space-time's geometry.

Atom interferometers such as AION and MAGIS-100 extend the search for quantum jitters by using atoms as sensitive probes. When a laser pulse hits an atom, the atom enters superposition, in which it is simultaneously in two different locations at once. It then travels along two separate paths before being recombined by a final pulse. If space-time fluctuates slightly differently along one path than the other, a measurable shift is detected in the atom's interference pattern.

The cold-atom preparation and trapping apparatus for the strontium atom source in Fermilab's Matter-wave Atomic Gradiometer Interferometric Sensor (MAGIS-100).

Another approach called BMV experiments (after the surnames of their independent developers Sougato Bose and his collaborators, Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral) take diamond nanocrystals weighing around a hundred-billonth of a kilogram and place them into a state of quantum superposition.

Painstakingly shielded from every possible electromagnetic and nuclear interaction, and placed at different distances from one another, the diamonds are put through a key test. If they emerge from the experiment with the electron states entangled, then gravity alone produced the entanglement.

That would be evidence that gravity can transmit quantum effects — something a classical gravitational field could not produce. And if gravity (the curvature of space-time) can exist in superposition, it could be a strong clue that space-time's geometry is woven out of quantum information. The challenge, so far, is in excluding all the other effects that may obscure the signal.

On cosmic scales, future gravitational wave observatories ‪—‬ including the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer ‪—‬ could scrutinize gravity at the first clues' source: around black holes. After two black holes merge, the resulting object settles down by emitting gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies and decay times. Einstein's theory makes precise predictions for this "ringdown," allowing researchers to search for discrepancies.

An artist's illustration for how the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect ripples in space-time created by merging black holes.

Such discrepancies could potentially point to the quantum nature of space-time near black holes. Interpreting them would require distinguishing between competing explanations ‪—‬ an unexpected signal could cryptically hint at space-time's underlying nature, but it wouldn't reveal a direct picture of its microscopic ingredients.

To identify the bits that make up the reality beneath space-time, scientists are also turning to quantum computers. By entangling many qubits in specific ways to mimic different models of emergent space-time, scientists could determine which mathematical models of the constituent bits are more likely.

"The study of many-body, highly entangled systems is where the future of this whole enterprise is," Forshaw said.

Precursor tests are already underway. In 2022, for example, Google's Sycamore quantum processor was used to reproduce the behavior of a simple theoretical wormhole — not by creating a real hole in space-time but by arranging nine qubits so that their behavior could also be described using gravity.

Earlier this year, researchers went further, using the trapped-ion quantum computer IonQ Forte to test how something resembling gravitational geometry could emerge from patterns of quantum information. The qubits in Forte were arranged into a model that could be interpreted in two connected ways: both as a network of quantum information and as a simple holographic geometry. The researchers then altered the entanglement between the qubits. In the model’s gravitational interpretation, this was akin to adding mass. Just as adding mass bends Einstein's space-time, the researchers expected changing the entanglement to alter the corresponding geometry — and it did.

The findings demonstrate that researchers can study a mathematical relationship between entanglement and geometry using quantum hardware. However, they do not establish that our space-time emerges from lower-dimensional quantum information.

"The experiment that we did is a baby step in that direction," Crystal Noel, an experimental physicist at Duke University who led the experimental side of the project, told Live Science. One limitation of this result is that it reproduces features of a simplified, static theoretical universe, rather than the expanding universe in which we live. Testing a more realistic model of the universe might require entangling 100 or 200 qubits, which may be possible in the near future.

Each of these experiments will probe different aspects of the relationship between gravity and quantum physics, although none would by itself prove that space-time emerges from information. Taken together, however, their results could begin to reveal what theories of quantum gravity match the real world — and whether emergent space-time is among them.

Such a discovery would raise profound questions not only about the universe’s foundations, but about what it means for anything — including ourselves — to exist within it.

"If I tell you that space doesn't exist, it really questions what it means to be," Forshaw said. "How can you actually talk about things when there's no space to put things in?"

Alex Keshavarzi is a senior research fellow in particle physics at University College London in the U.K., where he is probing how the behaviors of muons (the heavier cousins of electrons) could reveal unknown particles and forces. #6331. Dragonfly wings inspired a new way to build materials that can take a hit

Engineers took cues from dragonfly wings to 3D-print materials that spread damage and absorb energy when compressed.

A neat grid or honeycomb looks like the smartest way to build something light and strong, and engineers have borrowed both for decades. Squeeze a printed grid hard enough, though, and it fails the way a stack of cans does.

One row buckles, then the next, in a band that runs across the whole piece.

A leaf’s veins, a dragonfly’s wing and a spider’s web are built the opposite way, from struts of wildly different sizes tangled together.

Materials printed on that plan spread the damage out instead of concentrating it. They also absorbed as much energy as the tidy lattices, or more.

Engineers at MIT and network scientists at Northeastern University’s Network Science Institute designed the new materials, which they call scale-rich metamaterials.

So far the team has tested them as flat, credit-card-sized polymer plates in a lab, not as helmets or packaging.

“This is a completely new way of thinking for metamaterials,” said study author Carlos Portela, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT.

Metamaterials get their properties from their internal architecture rather than their chemistry. Engineers usually design one small building block, a unit cell, and repeat it over and over.

So every strut inside is about the same length and thickness.

Albert-László Barabási, a physicist at Northeastern, has spent his career mapping networks from the internet to the brain. Those networks don’t look like a grid at all.

The veins in a dragonfly’s wing run from about four thousandths of an inch (0.1 millimeters) to about two inches (50 millimeters) long.

Leaf veins and spider silk span a range at least as wide, and the struts inside bone vary tenfold in thickness.

Barabási asked whether that spread of sizes could be built into a solid material on purpose. He took the question to Portela’s lab, with a mathematician at Utrecht University in the Netherlands joining the team.

The team’s recipe is short. A computer picks a random point inside a square and draws a straight beam through it at a random angle, until the beam hits the edge.

The computer picks another point and draws another beam, which stops when it meets the first.

Each new beam is thinner than the last, by a rate the designer sets. Only two settings matter: how thick the first beam is and how fast the thickness shrinks.

The program repeats the step hundreds of times, so the last beams are short and fine while the first few stay long and thick.

The finished design has no typical strut. Lengths, thicknesses and the number of crossings per beam all run across orders of magnitude inside one sample, the same pattern network scientists find in road maps and food webs.

Changing those two settings also changes how stiff the material is in different directions. Across 2,600 computer-generated designs, the directional stiffness varied 24-fold.

That is far more range than a square grid, a honeycomb or a random foam-like Voronoi pattern can offer.

The researchers 3D-printed the designs in a stiff polymer. Each sample was a few inches across, with beams from a few thousandths of an inch up to an inch or so long.

Then they squeezed the samples in a press, alongside square, honeycomb and Voronoi samples of the same density, about 42% solid, three of each.

The square grid buckled first in a single row, and the collapse spread sideways across the whole sample before the next row went. The honeycomb formed wide crushed bands.

Even the random Voronoi foam compacted from the bottom up while its top stayed untouched.

The scale-rich samples didn’t do that. Their stress rose smoothly as the press pushed down, with no sudden drops, and the crushing stayed spread across the whole piece.

The team scored that spread on a scale where zero means perfectly even deformation and one means all the damage in one spot.

The new samples stayed at or below 0.2 even after being compressed by 25% of their original height.

The energy they soaked up before packing down matched or beat the three conventional designs.

“Because there is such a richness of length scales in these networked materials, if one part fails, there is a strong web of structures around it that keeps the entire material from failing catastrophically,” Portela said.

“It’s more efficient at distributing damage and absorbing energy.”

For a final test, the team borrowed from the thick, graded rind of a pomelo, denser toward the outside.

They generated a network whose beams crowded the edges and steered load around a disc of clear acrylic embedded in the middle.

Under compression, the acrylic disc inside a square or honeycomb lattice showed bands of stress under polarized light. Inside the scale-rich network, the bands were far fewer.

Computer simulations put the stress on the disc at as little as about one-fifth of the stress in the conventional lattices.

The same two settings can also tune how fast vibrations travel through the material. The team used that to design a lens that focuses sound waves, so far only in simulation.

Everything the team crushed was a flat plate of one polymer, printed at a resolution of about four thousandths of an inch.

The authors showed on paper that the recipe extends to three dimensions, with plates or beams instead of lines. The stiffness trends carry over, but those 3D versions were simulated rather than squeezed.

The study didn’t test the materials as any product. Helmets, armor, packaging and crash parts are the uses the authors named, and each would need its own tests at full size.

The group has posted its generator code publicly. The authors wrote that a design needing only two inputs is well suited to AI-driven searches for structures with a target stiffness or energy absorption.

Future studies could run those searches, and print the 3D versions to see whether the even crushing holds in a solid block.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6330. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6328. LSD changes the brain’s rhythm in a way earlier studies missed

Brain recordings from 17 volunteers show that LSD speeds up two brain rhythms even as it weakens them.

Brain recordings of people on psychedelics have told the same story for years: the brain’s steady electrical rhythms get weaker, as if the drug were turning the volume down.

A new analysis of recordings from 17 people given LSD finds that the volume isn’t the whole story. The drug also turns up the tempo.

LSD pushes two of the brain’s main rhythms to faster beats, and it makes the brain’s electrical activity more detailed and less predictable.

Venkatesh Subramani, a doctoral student at the Université de Montréal, led the analysis with his supervisor Karim Jerbi. Jerbi is a psychology professor there and a researcher at Mila, the Quebec artificial intelligence institute.

Co-authors included Nicolas Farrugia and Giulia Lioi of IMT Atlantique in France and Robin Carhart-Harris of the University of California, San Francisco.

“Imagine a radio station switching its broadcast frequency from 99.5 to 100.5 FM,” Jerbi said.

“If your radio stays tuned to 99.5, the signal may seem distorted or lost. In the same way, overlooking the shift to faster brain rhythms can lead us to misinterpret LSD’s effects on the brain.”

Groups of neurons firing together produce rhythms that a sensor outside the head can pick up. Researchers call them brain waves.

Alpha waves dominate when you rest with your eyes closed. Beta waves are faster and show up during concentration and decision-making.

Under psychedelics those waves look weaker, and the standard reading is that neurons are firing less in unison. Subramani’s team pointed out a catch.

If a rhythm speeds up, its peak can shift outside the frequency range researchers are measuring. That shift can make the wave look weaker even if its strength hasn’t changed.

So the team pulled the two possibilities apart. They first stripped out the brain’s rhythm-free background activity.

Then they located each person’s actual alpha and beta peaks under LSD and under placebo, and measured the power at those peaks.

The recordings were made at Imperial College London by Carhart-Harris’s group. Seventeen healthy volunteers came in twice, two weeks apart.

In one session, they received an intravenous injection of 75 micrograms of LSD, roughly the weight of a grain of salt. In the other they received a saline placebo, without being told which was which.

About four hours after the injection, each person lay in a magnetoencephalography scanner. It records the faint magnetic fields that neurons produce, with timing down to the millisecond.

They rested with their eyes closed for seven minutes, and in a separate seven-minute block they listened to ambient music.

The Montreal team reanalyzed those recordings with newer signal-processing tools and a machine-learning model trained to tell the LSD sessions from the placebo sessions.

Under LSD, alpha waves ran about 2 cycles per second faster than on placebo, and beta waves about 5 cycles per second faster, across large areas of the cortex. The waves did also weaken.

Once the speed-up was accounted for, that weakening held up as real rather than an artifact of looking in the wrong place.

The two effects didn’t fully overlap. The weakening was strongest in regions that handle hearing, language, and emotion.

The speed-up followed its own map, and the regions that weakened most tended to speed up least.

Anesthetics do the opposite to the alpha rhythm, slowing it down as the cortex becomes less excitable. The authors read the faster alpha under LSD as a sign of a more excitable cortex.

They also noted that psilocybin and DMT haven’t been shown to shift the peaks this way, so the speed-up may be a signature specific to LSD.

A fractal is a shape that repeats itself in its own parts, the way each floret of a Romanesco broccoli is a smaller broccoli.

The team measured how fractal the brain signal was over time, and how varied its patterns were. Both rose under LSD.

The increases were largest in areas tied to vision, hearing, memory, and mental imagery, and smallest in the motor cortex.

That split fits a familiar feature of the drug. Perception and inner experience change a great deal, while people can still move normally.

People on LSD often report seeing repeating geometric patterns with their eyes closed. The paper links the two only loosely.

“Our findings lend support to this intriguing hypothesis, but they do not yet confirm it,” Jerbi said. “We measure the fractal structure of brain signals over time, not the fractal structure of the images people perceive.”

Given only the shift in peak frequencies, the machine-learning model identified the LSD session more than 82% of the time.

Models trained on the fractal and complexity measures did almost as well. The brain regions the models relied on matched the ones the conventional statistics had flagged.

“Our machine-learning algorithm can distinguish brain states under LSD from those under placebo using brain signals alone,” Subramani said.

“By examining the clues it relies on, we can identify LSD’s signatures in brain activity.”

Music, which is routinely played during psychedelic therapy, didn’t amplify any of these effects. If anything the trend ran the other way, with slightly smaller brain changes during the music block.

That difference didn’t survive the statistical correction, and the authors called it exploratory.

Seventeen people is a small group, and everyone received a single dose while healthy, so the study says nothing about whether any of this helps patients.

The volunteers rated their experience at the peak of the drug’s effect, while the scanner ran about two and a half hours later.

The authors wrote that this gap may be why brain changes and reported experiences lined up only loosely.

The recordings also included no direct measure of muscle activity, which can contaminate the fastest brain signals. So the authors treated their high-frequency results with extra caution.

The next question is whether the speed-up really belongs to LSD alone.

Subramani and his colleagues are now running the same analysis on recordings taken under psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and under DMT.

The aim is to see whether the three drugs produce the same signatures in the brain or different ones.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

#6327. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 19: Mercury moves into Libra

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 18: The Leonid meteor shower peaks

The solar system is a dynamic place. Let’s return to the predawn sky today to check out the inner planets’ progress relative to the stars of Virgo. An hour before sunrise, both Mercury and Venus are again well above the eastern horizon, with the stars around them still visible before twilight brightens too much.

Compared with earlier in the week, Venus now sits to the upper left of Spica, rather than directly above it. Venus will pass 1.8° due north of Spica later today at 6 P.M. EST. Now moving steadily east, it will track along the ecliptic, slowly headed for Libra. Mercury has already reached the Balance, sitting within its domain and to the far lower left of Kappa (κ) Virginis, as opposed to the pair’s close proximity a few days ago.

Pull out your telescope to see how the planets’ appearances have changed, too. Mercury is now 55% lit and 7” across, while Venus is 18% lit and has shrunk more noticeably, now 47” across.

#6326. Wind turbines may have killed nearly 19 million bats in the U.S. since 1981

A new study draws on decades of wind farm surveys to estimate how many bats turbines killed across the lower 48 states from 1981 to 2024.

The bats that die under wind turbines are picked up one carcass at a time, by crews walking the ground under each tower.

For decades, those site-by-site counts were the main tally anyone had.

Combining those counts with a statistical model, researchers estimated that wind turbines killed about 18.7 million bats in the lower 48 states from 1981 through the end of the study period.

Since 2021, the toll has run above 1.5 million a year. That is a scale the authors wrote may rival the fungal disease that has devastated cave-hibernating bats.

Charles Labuzzetta of the U.S. Geological Survey‘s Fort Collins Science Center led the analysis with colleagues at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Laboratory of the Rockies.

The figures are model estimates with wide ranges, built from monitoring that was never designed to be added up, and the relationships they found are correlations, not proven causes.

In an interview with Earth.com, Labuzzetta said the data behind the study were richer than their patchy origins suggest.

“We found that there could still be a lot to learn from the rich monitoring data that has been collected since the late 1990s and continues to be collected,” he noted.

The team pulled together 499 monitoring reports from 277 wind facilities in the lower 48 states, filed with the Fish and Wildlife Service since the late 1990s.

Each report counted the carcasses found under turbines and estimated how many were missed. But the searches differed in length, area and method, and many reports are confidential.

A statistical model pooled them, corrected for what the searchers could not see, and projected fatalities back to 1981.

The median came out at 18,696,140 bats across ten species, with a plausible range of about 13.3 million to 25.7 million.

That is the estimate for the lower 48 states that the compliance reports could never produce on their own.

Four species account for nearly all of it. The authors estimate about 6.7 million hoary bats, 5.8 million eastern red bats, 3.4 million silver-haired bats and 1.5 million big brown bats.

On average, a turbine killed close to six hoary bats a year. At the other end, the rare Indiana bat accounted for about 6,000 deaths over the whole period.

The last national figures date from 2013, and they put the toll in the hundreds of thousands a year.

Those estimates leaned on a single rule of thumb, about 1.7 hoary bats per megawatt of capacity.

A projection built on it assumed roughly 113,000 hoary bat deaths in 2012, and the new model estimates about 268,000 for that year. The old figure was less than half the new one.

The gap matters because of what the old projection, built on expert judgment, already said.

Run on the lower numbers, it warned that hoary bats could lose 50% to 90% of their population within 50 years. Eastern red bats have been dying faster still, more than 500,000 a year since 2021.

Rated capacity, the usual yardstick, turned out to be a poor predictor of deaths. The area swept by the blades was a better predictor.

On most turbines built since 2020 that is 2.5 to 5 acres (10,000 to 20,000 square meters).

Researchers estimated more deaths among several bat species at turbines whose blades swept a larger area or passed closer to the ground.

For all ten species, estimated deaths were higher at wind farms closer to rivers. The study couldn’t determine whether being near a river was itself responsible for the higher toll.

Labuzzetta told Earth.com those patterns point to siting and design as levers, but not to a single fix.

“There is still a great deal to learn about what strategies may be optimal and could provide the greatest conservation management return on investment for individual species and across all species,” he said.

White-nose syndrome, a fungal disease first seen in 2006, has cut some cave-hibernating species by more than 90%.

The authors compared their total with one rough estimate of the disease’s losses and found the two comparable in size.

The two threats mostly hit different bats. The disease kills bats that hibernate in caves, while turbines mostly kill the migratory tree-roosting species.

Across North American bats as a whole, the authors wrote, the two may compound.

Whether 18.7 million deaths translate into shrinking populations is the question the study can’t answer.

Data on how many hoary or eastern red bats exist, how long they live and how fast they breed are largely unavailable, the authors wrote. So the same number of deaths could mean a crisis or a dent.

“Our research alone cannot answer whether fatalities from wind energy are leading to similar population-level declines for migratory tree-roosting bat species,” Labuzzetta said.

Population trends from the North American Bat Monitoring Program could begin to fill that gap.

The authors also called for monitoring at wind farms to be collected and shared in a form that can be pooled.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Before an asteroid slammed into Earth 66 million years ago, dinosaurs had roamed our planet for more than 160 million years.

They emerged around 230 million to 240 million years ago, during the Triassic period, when the supercontinent Pangaea had united the landmasses. As Pangaea broke apart, dinosaurs went on to inhabit continents all over the world, including what became Antarctica, which was a temperate rainforest during the Cretaceous period.

Dinosaurs lived in diverse ecosystems, from the snowy Arctic to the hot equatorial regions of Gondwana, a supercontinent in the Southern Hemisphere. As dinosaurs evolved in their different environments, they developed distinct defenses and adaptations to help them survive.

#6324. A giant planet stopped crossing its star while astronomers watched, and it never left

Astronomers saw a planet around a single star stop crossing it, a first. A hidden neighbor is likely tipping its orbit.

Astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years. Then, in March 2026, it stopped showing up.

The planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere. Its orbit has tipped, most likely from the pull of a second planet in the same system, one that astronomers haven’t detected directly.

TOI-2535 b, more than 1,000 light-years away, is the first confirmed planet around a single star that astronomers have seen stop crossing. Samuel Yee, a 51 Pegasi b Postdoctoral Fellow at UCLA, led the work with UCLA astrophysicist Erik Petigura.

Each of those crossings is called a transit. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching,” Yee said.

When a planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight. The star dims for a few hours, and that small dip is how NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) finds new worlds.

A transit only shows up if the star, the planet and Earth line up almost perfectly. If the orbit tips by just a few degrees, the planet passes above or below the star as seen from Earth, and the star never dims.

TESS checked on the star, called TOI-2535, five times between April 2019 and March 2026.

The planet orbiting it is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. It goes around once every 8.24 days. Mercury takes 88 days, more than 10 times as long.

To confirm the planet, the team used an instrument on the 11.5-foot (3.5-meter) WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona. It tracked how the star shifted back and forth, and the measurements ruled out a small star.

Most planets that cross their stars keep a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b’s crossings came as much as six hours early or late. No hot Jupiter that circles its star in under 10 days has a bigger timing swing on record.

Each crossing was also a little shorter than the last, and each one dimmed the star a little less.

A planet blocks less light, for less time, as its path moves from the middle of a star toward its edge.

Over seven years, the path likely moved across more than half of the star’s face. It passed the middle, grazed the edge, then missed the star entirely.

From the ground, the team tried 15 times and caught a crossing only six times, because the planet kept arriving when it wasn’t expected.

When TESS looked again in March 2026, it found no crossing anywhere in the window where the planet could have shown up.

So what’s pulling on it? Planets in the same system tug on each other. If two orbits are tilted relative to one another, those tugs slowly swing the direction each orbit faces.

The team’s computer models suggest the neighbor is at least as massive as Saturn, so it’s probably a second giant planet. The two likely move in a simple rhythm, such as one circling twice for every lap of the other.

By the models, the two orbits must be tilted at least 5 degrees apart to turn this fast.

In most tightly packed systems, orbits stay within 1 to 2 degrees of each other. If this tilt holds up, the system will be one of only a handful so far out of line.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits,” Yee said.

“We know of a few systems that are like this. This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly.”

Petigura used Earth’s moon to explain it.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura said.

“But because the moon’s orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon’s orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.”

The same geometry decides when TOI-2535 b will be back. The team calculated that each orbit goes through a full cycle every 30 to 50 years.

The researchers expect the planet to start crossing its star again within that span. Its hidden neighbor could start crossing even sooner.

Early planet formation models suggested giant planets need lots of ice to form. So hot Jupiters probably formed far from their stars and moved closer later.

How? Yee and Petigura see two ways. One is violent. A near-collision knocks the planet onto a stretched-out orbit, and the star pulls it in.

The other is slow. The planet drifts inward with other planets through the gas and dust around a young star. This way should leave the orbits flat.

TOI-2535 b has a close giant neighbor, so it couldn’t have come the violent way, the team wrote.

“Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,” Yee said. “We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting.”

The tilt is still a loose end. The researchers think parts of the system may have tugged on each other later, tipping the orbits over time.

Hundreds of hot Jupiters are known around other stars. Few have a planet close enough to change their orbits. When one does, the neighbor is almost always much smaller. The only other known exception is WASP-148.

The team can’t say how massive the neighbor is or where it orbits. The crossing times also scattered more than the models predicted.

The star’s back-and-forth motion was jumpier than expected for an old, calm star, too. Both clues could mean there’s more than one unseen planet.

TESS’s first four years of data alone couldn’t have clearly shown the shrinking crossings.

With no crossings left to time, the researchers wrote that the best way forward is to measure the star’s back-and-forth motion often. A neighbor as heavy as the models suggest should show up in that data on its own.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#6323. A brain region known for listening helps us speak

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Recordings reveal how Wernicke’s area helps turn thoughts into words

A small bit of brain has big roles in understanding and producing speech, a new study finds.

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

A. Silva et al. A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area. Science, 2026. doi: 10.1126/science.aef8963.

Laura Sanders is the neuroscience writer. She holds a Ph.D. in molecular biology from the University of Southern California.

#6322. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column

Thursday, November 19Sunrise: 6:50 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 1:41 P.M.Moonset: 1:07 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

Sunrise: 6:52 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:29 P.M.Moonset: 3:22 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%)

Sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:59 P.M.Moonset: 4:34 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%)

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus, also in Taurus, at 2 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 4:24 P.M.Moonset: 7:10 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%)

Wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 5:24 P.M.Moonset: 8:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%)

Thursday, November 26Sunrise: 6:58 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 6:35 P.M.Moonset: 9:33 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%)

Friday, November 27Sunrise: 6:59 A.M.Sunset: 4:36 P.M.Moonrise: 7:53 P.M.Moonset: 10:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6321. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6320. Nov. 19, 1969: Apollo 12 lands on the Moon

Five days after their Nov. 14, 1969, launch amid stormy skies, Apollo 12’s Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum (the Ocean of Storms). Part of Apollo 12’s mission was to demonstrate improvements to the precision of lunar landings, and Conrad piloted the Intrepid Lunar Module to a pinpoint landing on Nov. 19. While their crewmate Richard Gordon remained in the Command Module (Yankee Clipper) above them, Conrad and Bean began the first of their two moonwalks. Conrad descended the ladder from the LM first, and as he stepped onto the Moon quipped, “Whoopie! Man, that may have been a small one for Neil, but that’s a long one for me.”

Although Bean accidentally pointed their color TV camera at the Sun, damaging it, both the Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) were otherwise successful. The astronauts collected rock and soil samples and deployed their Apollo Lunar Surface Experiment Package (ALSEP), which included a solar wind collector, and seismometer, and a magnetometer. They also visited the Surveyor 3 unmanned lander (which had been on the Moon since 1967), retrieving several components of the spacecraft to return to Earth for study. After 31 and a half hours on the Moon, nearly eight hours of those spent in EVAs, Intrepid lifted off and re-docked with Yankee Clipper. The crew safely splashed down back on Earth on Nov. 24.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Astronomers have found two rare asteroids trailing Neptune in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data. The rocks, called Neptune's L5 Trojans, could illuminate the conditions of the infant solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered two ancient Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune ‪—‬ the first new ones to be spotted in 15 years.

The findings, published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could improve our understanding of the early solar system while reinforcing the Rubin Observatory's potential to unearth new cosmic objects during its brisk scans of the sky.

Trojan asteroids are icy, rocky bodies that dwell in a planet's vicinity but don't orbit it. Instead, these asteroids orbit the sun, following the same path as the planet. Trojan asteroids exist in distinct swarms roughly 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, called Lagrange points 4 and 5 (L4 and L5), respectively, the gravitational tugs of the sun and the planet balance each other, essentially "locking" the asteroids in position, according to NASA.

However, very few Trojans actually hang around for billions of years. Such asteroids are likely planetary building block remnants from the solar system's infancy, and detecting them in the outer solar system can be challenging.

Jupiter's Trojans are the most famous; the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center notes that an incredible 15,000 of these objects have been discovered so far. But some other planets, including Neptune, also host Trojans. In fact, a 2005 study suggested that Neptune has up to 10 times more Trojans than Jupiter. Until now, though, astronomers have spotted only 28 Neptunian Trojans, with just two of these being long-term L5 members.

There are two reasons why it's difficult to detect these rocks. First, the Neptunian Trojans are extremely faint. More critically, for nearly 15 years, the Trojan population's position in the sky relative to Earth has overlapped with the central region of the Milky Way. Consequently, bright background stars have made it nearly impossible to discern the tiny, faint asteroids, Megan Schwamb, the study's first author and a researcher who focuses on how planets and their building blocks form and evolve at Queen's University Belfast, told Live Science in an email.

An illustration of the Jovian Trojans orbiting in front of and behind Jupiter

However, from 2025 onward, the L5 group's position has moved — albeit extremely slowly — away from the galactic plane. This has made the population slightly easier to observe. At the same time, the Rubin Observatory started scanning the entire Southern Hemisphere sky with the world's largest digital camera.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Rubin is pretty uniquely suited to being excellent at discovering Neptune Trojans," study co-author Kathryn Volk, a scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, told Live Science in an email. "The on-sky density of these objects is not particularly high, so having a large field of view helps a lot!" (Rubin has a field of view equivalent to seven full moons, according to the observatory's website.) This, along with the observatory's excellent vision — which allows it to detect objects 100 billion times dimmer than Venus — enabled the discovery of the new Trojans.

The new Trojan observations form part of the Rubin Science Validation Survey, a three-month-long test run that was held in mid-2025 prior to the start of the observatory's flagship decade-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which is now underway. By chance, the Science Validation Survey encompassed the part of the sky containing Neptune's L5 Trojans, leading to the asteroids being photographed within three weeks of the survey's start.

Following the discoveries, the researchers created computer models to determine the asteroids' orbits. These simulations revealed that the duo will continue to tag behind Neptune for a billion years. The results suggest that the asteroids' trajectories have been stable for several billion years, which means the asteroids may have been traversing these routes from the time of the early solar system. The researchers also found a third object in Rubin's data, but it had a stable orbit in only some of their simulations, leading them to classify it as a candidate Trojan rather than a confirmed one.

However, the two confirmed Trojans likely didn't form in place alongside Neptune. The simulations showed that the asteroids' orbits are highly tilted, just like those of the previously discovered L5 asteroids — suggesting that Neptune captured these objects as they were hurtling past.

Determining the properties of both the Jovian and Neptunian Trojan asteroids will help researchers understand what happened during the solar system's infancy, when the giant planets are believed to have migrated to their present-day positions, Volk said.

Schwamb expects the LSST to unveil many more of the hypothesized Neptunian Trojans, especially because it will survey this same patch of the sky repeatedly over the next several months.

#6318. Hear stars being born in Chandra’s new sonifications

Every image of the cosmos is a translation of data. The X-rays collected by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the infrared light gathered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are invisible to our eyes, so astronomers assign them colors we can see. Even optical observations, from Hubble to backyard astrophotographers, translate, too, often assigning or enhancing color based on emission in various filters.

Sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone. The idea dates back at least to the Geiger counter, invented in 1908, whose clicks intensify as radiation climbs. In 2020, the Chandra X-ray Center launched A Universe of Sound, NASA’s first ongoing program to sonify astronomical data.

Our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide. Sonification also opens the cosmos to people who are blind or have low vision, for whom a processed image offers little.

RELATED: Listen to the universe: How sonification turns data into sound

On November 17, Chandra released four new sonifications, each built on a region where stars are forming right now. Young, massive stars blast out X-rays in fierce winds and outbursts, and studying those nurseries helps astronomers reconstruct how stars — the Sun included — got their start. Each piece pairs Chandra’s X-ray data with views from other NASA telescopes.

Each sonification plays as a short video. A line sweeps across the image, and whatever it crosses becomes sound. Most of the regions also come in three versions — Chandra’s X-rays alone, the companion telescope’s data alone, and the full composite. Try a single layer first, then the composite, and you’ll start to hear which sounds are associated with which kind of light.

At around 400 light-years away, the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex is the closest star-forming region of the four. This crowded region is filled with a wide variety of stars. Chandra’s X-ray data identifies individual newborn stars, while JWST maps the other stars, gas, and dust around them. The X-rays ring out as bright, shimmering notes. Meanwhile, the clouds of dust and gas provide shifting ethereal chords, and individual stars land as crisp, percussive pings. Listen for the hush partway through — that’s a stretch of dark dust that hides almost all light.

About 1,310 light-years away and just below Orion’s Belt, the Orion Nebula is often visible to the naked eye and shows up in even the smallest telescope on a dark night. Chandra reveals more than 1,000 young stars here, each one sparkling in the sonification. Around them, the nebula’s diffuse X-ray glow holds steady as a ringing whistle. JWST’s infrared view of the dust and gas is audible as bent, warbling strings and a synthesized harp, reaching a crescendo in the nebula’s densest region before fading out.

Roughly 7,670 light-years away lies the ridge of gas and dust that became one of JWST’s most famous images when it was released in 2022. Chandra sees the scene differently, cutting through the dust to the hidden infant stars within it. Each of those stars plays as a quick stab, while the region’s faint X-ray glow draws out droning, unhurried notes — all played on an actual cello by musician Johnny Mok. JWST’s towering cliffs are a steady drone underneath, with new instruments chiming in briefly to denote a star or one of the cliffline’s jagged peaks.

Some 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, M82 is the only object in the album beyond our galaxy. This starburst galaxy is building stars many times faster than the Milky Way. Its newborn giants burn out and explode quickly, venting superheated gas plumes that shine brightly in Chandra’s X-rays. Here, Chandra’s data joins Hubble’s visible-light view and infrared from JWST and the retired Spitzer Space Telescope. X-rays sit at the very top of the register, with the region’s busy center whooshing like moving air, filling most of the audible spectrum. It is punctuated by sharp, short stings from brighter newborn stars. The infrared rumbles below as a low hum interrupted by picked notes, and visible light fills the middle with a variety of sounds, including sweeping chords that rise and fall with optical brightness.

The Chandra sonifications come from a team led by visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand of the Chandra X-ray Center, working with astrophysicist Matt Russo and musician Andrew Santaguida of the SYSTEM Sounds project and consultant Christine Malec, a blind astronomer and musician. You can hear all four at the Chandra release page, and find the program’s full back catalog at chandra.si.edu/sound.

Where Chandra’s new album is composed by others, Skysynth lets you become the composer. Built by the same SYSTEM Sounds duo of Russo and Santaguida for the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s SkyViewer app, it lets you roam Rubin’s ultra-wide view of the southern sky — press Play to coast, or steer with your arrow keys or by dragging with the mouse. Galaxies crossing the center of the screen strum a harp and stars ring a glockenspiel, with color setting the pitch and brightness the volume.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.
